sections.heading: Choose by workflow specificity
sections.content: She does not describe build-versus-buy as an all-or-nothing choice. A more specific internal workflow may justify building your own agent; for more generalizable needs, she suggests getting something off the shelf. She also warns that many narrow AI tools can proliferate—potentially leaving a company procuring 20 tools for 20 jobs instead of using an integrated platform.

sections.heading: Why try building internally
sections.content: Her rationale is that an agent’s value can depend on a company’s esoteric context, content, and workflow, and the space is still nascent. She says building can be easier and cheaper than expected and may produce returns quickly. As an example, Vercel’s lead agent took six weeks with one person spending a third of their time, while a lost-deal bot had an initial version in about two days (roughly 40 hours); the lead agent was estimated to cost about $1,000 a year to run. She presents these as examples, not guarantees, and says better-integrated agent platforms may ultimately emerge.

sections.heading: What Vercel’s build involved
sections.content: Vercel’s sales engineers built agents directly on the Vercel platform and wrote code. Grosser points to its AI Gateway for calling different models, sandbox for running untrusted code, workflows for processes, and fluid compute for using compute efficiently when needed. She credits the platform with helping the team get agents into production rapidly.
